item.title: The Impact of Conspiracy Thinking on Well-Being
item.description:
Conspiracy Theories

The Impact of Conspiracy Thinking on Well-Being

A shocking number of people endorse some form of conspiracy theory.

Posted August 1, 2026

Key points
  • Conspiracy theories are linked with lower life satisfaction.
  • Such theories are also associated with searching for meaning.
  • The tendency to endorse conspiracy theories may be related to a threat-focused cognitive processing style.

Do you have a friend or loved one who believes in conspiracy theories? According to a 2017 study published in the Journal of Social Psychiatry and Psychiatric Epidemiology, the chances that you do are quite high. The study's authors report that over a quarter of the 5645 American adults surveyed endorsed some form of conspiracy theory. Some researchers estimate that as much as one-third of people may endorse some form of conspiracy theory.

Some conspiracy theories may seem harmless enough at first glance. Something is endearing about the kitschy Bigfoot-sighting maps available at gas stations in the Pacific Northwest and images of little green men in flying saucers flying over the Nevada desert. Unfortunately, conspiracy theories are not all kitschy fun; they often lead to racist and antisemitic explanations for a wide variety of social problems.

In a 2026 article published in Applied Cognitive Psychology, psychologist Andrew Denovan and his co-authors explain that a core aspect of conspiracy theories is that they “attribute major events or circumstances to the coordinated, purposeful, and covert actions of powerful actors,” challenging mainstream institutional narratives.

While the vast majority of these challenges to mainstream narratives are totally false, conspiracy theorists have been proven correct on occasion. One example of an event that is now widely accepted as real but was once dismissed as conspiracy is the MKUltra experiments, a Cold War-era program of research that aimed to create super soldiers and mind control techniques. The victims of the MKUltra experiments were subjected to psychological torture. Similarly, Watergate, the political scandal involving illegal wiretapping of the Democratic National Convention, is now widely accepted as fact, but was once thought of as a conspiracy.

Conspiracy theorists are often portrayed as isolated loners, with little going for them—like Jesse Plemons’ recent portrayal of Teddy Gatz in the film Begonia. But if as much as a third of people endorse conspiracy theories, your average conspiracy theorist is unlikely to be much like the isolated misanthrope that might come to mind when we imagine them.

What impact does endorsing conspiracy theories have on believers?

Denovan and his team wanted to investigate the relationship between believing in conspiracy theories and self-evaluation, meaning, and life satisfaction. They reasoned that conspiracy theorists believe malicious and powerful forces surround them, and they likely have a threat-focused cognitive processing style. Threat-focused cognitive processing is associated with reduced self-esteem, meaning, and life satisfaction; the study's authors hypothesized that individuals who endorse conspiracy theories would also be lower on these variables.

They sampled 615 participants in the United Kingdom, ages 19 to 82, every two months for eight months. They found that higher levels of conspiratorial ideation were associated with more pessimism and less self-esteem. Pessimism and low self-esteem were associated with less presence of meaning in life; however, conspiratorial ideation was associated with more presence of meaning in life and search for meaning in life. The presence of meaning in life was associated with more life satisfaction, whereas lower self-esteem and search for meaning in life were associated with less life satisfaction.

While the relationship between conspiracy theory and life satisfaction is complicated, overall, the endorsement of conspiracy theory was linked to lower levels of life satisfaction. However, the study's authors caution that their study's design cannot show causality.

Why might someone believe in a conspiracy theory? It seems that while conspiracy theories are associated with lower overall life satisfaction, they could also increase a sense of meaning in life in some cases. Believing in conspiracy theories may also help provide a sense of community. Furthermore, conspiracy theories have occasionally been proven correct. The conspiracist may also interpret the negative consequences of their theories as being further evidence for their convictions. In the mind of the conspiracy theorists, lower life satisfaction may be a natural consequence of having taken the “red pill” or refused their dose of “Soma.”

Denovan and his co-authors have a few suggestions for combating conspiracy thinking. They suggest that interventions aimed at improving self-esteem and fostering meaning in life may help break the patterns of thinking that lead to such theories.

item.title: How Coffee Affects Mood and Cognition Via the Gut-Brain Axis
item.description:
Gut-Brain Axis

How Coffee Affects Mood and Cognition Via the Gut-Brain Axis

Research suggests coffee impacts mental health through pathways beyond caffeine.

Posted August 1, 2026

Key points
  • Coffee altered gut microbes and metabolites linked to mood and cognition.
  • Some microbiome changes occurred with both caffeinated and decaf coffee.
  • Caffeine aided alertness, while decaf showed possible memory benefits.
Source: Gideon Putra / Pixabay

Coffee is often treated as a simple delivery system for caffeine. We drink it to feel more awake, improve concentration, and overcome the mental drag of an early morning or afternoon slump.

But coffee contains hundreds of biologically active compounds, including polyphenols, alkaloids, and fiber-like substances that interact with the digestive system. A new study suggests that coffee may also influence mental functioning by changing the gut microbiome and the chemical signals passing between the digestive tract and the brain.

While the findings do not establish that coffee can be used to treat depression, anxiety, or cognitive impairment, they do suggest that the psychological effects of coffee are more complicated than the temporary stimulation produced by caffeine.

The Microbiota-Gut-Brain Axis

The digestive tract and brain communicate continuously through what scientists call the microbiota-gut-brain axis.

This bidirectional network includes the vagus nerve, immune system, hormones, microbial metabolites, and neurotransmitter-related chemicals. Gut bacteria help process components of our diet and produce substances that may influence inflammation, stress responses, mood, and cognition.

That does not mean that individual bacteria determine how we feel or think. The microbiome is a complex ecosystem shaped by diet, medication, sleep, stress, genetics, and many other influences. But accumulating evidence suggests that food and beverages can alter microbial activity in ways that may eventually affect the brain.

Coffee is a particularly interesting candidate because it contains compounds that reach the colon, where they can be metabolized by gut microbes. Its polyphenols and roasting-derived compounds may act somewhat like prebiotics, providing substrates that certain microbes can use.

What the Study Did

Researchers at University College Cork compared 31 habitual coffee drinkers with 31 people who did not regularly drink coffee. Habitual drinkers generally consumed three to five cups per day.

Participants completed measures of mood, stress, impulsivity, attention, memory, and other aspects of cognition. Researchers also analyzed stool and urine samples to study gut bacteria and microbial and coffee-related metabolites. The habitual coffee drinkers then stopped drinking coffee for two weeks. After this washout period, they were randomly assigned to reintroduce either caffeinated or decaffeinated coffee for three weeks.

The study reported that coffee drinkers had a measurably different gut microbial composition. They showed higher relative levels of bacteria from the Cryptobacterium and Eggerthella groups, along with differences in several microbial metabolites, including indole-related compounds and gamma-aminobutyric acid, or GABA.

Some metabolic changes shifted during coffee abstinence, suggesting that at least part of coffee’s influence on the gut may be reversible. Reintroducing coffee produced additional changes in the microbiome, and some occurred regardless of whether the coffee contained caffeine.

Source: beauty_of_nature / Pixabay

Coffee Is More Than Caffeine

Caffeine affects the brain primarily by blocking adenosine receptors, reducing the perception of sleep pressure and increasing alertness. But the study found that caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee produced distinct and sometimes complementary effects.

According to the researchers’ analyses, caffeinated coffee was associated with greater attention and alertness after reintroduction. The caffeine group also showed lower anxiety in this particular experiment. Decaffeinated coffee, meanwhile, was associated with improvements in aspects of learning and memory. Both groups reported changes consistent with better mood, including lower perceived stress and depressive symptoms.

These findings suggest that caffeine is not the only coffee component capable of affecting the brain. Polyphenols and their metabolites may influence inflammation, vascular function, cellular stress, or microbial activity. The microbiome may also determine how efficiently different people metabolize those compounds, helping explain why individuals can respond differently to the same beverage.

The researchers developed an integrated model identifying nine metabolites—including caffeine, theophylline, and several phenolic acids—that were strongly connected with particular microbes and cognitive measures. That does not demonstrate that the metabolites caused the cognitive changes, but it provides possible biological links for future study.

The Results Were Not Entirely Positive

The study’s findings were more nuanced than the idea that coffee simply creates a healthier gut and happier brain.

At the initial comparison, habitual coffee drinkers showed greater impulsivity and emotional reactivity, while non-coffee drinkers performed better on certain memory measures.

Several explanations are possible. Habitual coffee consumption may influence these traits, but people who are naturally more impulsive, emotionally reactive, fatigued, or stimulation-seeking may also be more likely to drink coffee. Caffeine withdrawal and tolerance can further complicate comparisons between habitual drinkers and people who rarely consume it.

The study therefore does not establish that coffee uniformly improves mental health or cognitive performance. Instead, it shows a changing pattern of biological and behavioral effects that depends on habitual use, abstinence, caffeine content, and possibly each person’s microbiome.

Coffee Is Not Mental Health Care

Based on this study, people should not begin drinking coffee to treat depression, anxiety, or memory problems. Caffeine can worsen anxiety, panic, insomnia, palpitations, and gastrointestinal symptoms. In people vulnerable to mania or hypomania, excessive caffeine and the resulting sleep disruption may contribute to mood destabilization.

Decaffeinated coffee may provide some coffee compounds without the same stimulant burden, but it is not entirely caffeine-free and may still cause digestive symptoms in susceptible people.

The new research offers a more interesting conclusion than “coffee is good for you.” Coffee appears to be a complex dietary exposure that interacts with microbes, metabolism, and brain function through several pathways, some of which are dependent on caffeine and others that apparently are not.

Ultimately, this study suggests that our morning cup may influence more than wakefulness. It may reshape an ongoing conversation between the microbes in our gut and the circuits in our brain.

item.title: Does AI Make Teams Better at Working Together?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Does AI Make Teams Better at Working Together?

How a team uses AI matters more than how powerful it is.

Posted August 1, 2026

Key points
  • Trust determines whether AI strengthens a team's creativity or fuels conflict within it.
  • The highest-performing groups treat AI output as something to verify, not something to copy.
  • AI helps most when it combines real-time participation with feedback and reflection.

Co-authored by Rónan Fulton, Alana McCarthy, and Michael Hogan.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly becoming part of collaborative learning. As GenAI tools become increasingly capable, discussion often centres on the technology itself: whether it will improve learning or undermine it. Yet this framing overlooks a more fundamental issue. Consider a surgical team. Access to sophisticated instruments does not determine whether an operation is successful. The outcome depends on how well the team communicates, coordinates, and trusts one another while using those tools. AI-supported collaborative learning is no different: Like a scalpel, AI proves its worth only in skilled, trusting hands.

Three recent empirical studies, involving more than 480 learners across higher education, suggest that the effectiveness of AI depends less on what the technology can do than on how people work with it. Together, they point towards an important conclusion: Designing AI for collaborative learning is not simply a technical challenge, but also a psychological one.

Interpersonal trust shapes the value of AI-supported collaboration

Luo and colleagues (2025) surveyed 308 university students working in 66 collaborative groups to investigate how trust, collective efficacy, and task conflict influenced team creativity when generative AI was introduced. Rather than treating collaboration as a single outcome, the study examined the social conditions that determine whether AI benefits group work. Trust was measured through students' perceptions of whether group members could openly discuss difficulties, approach tasks professionally, and rely on one another to fulfill their responsibilities. Task conflict reflected disagreements about how work should be organized, and whether AI-generated suggestions or human judgment should guide decisions.

The findings reveal AI's double-edged influence on collaboration. Students who perceived AI as intelligent developed stronger collective efficacy, a shared confidence in their group's ability to succeed, which in turn promoted team creativity. At the same time, AI also increased task conflict, creating disagreements that reduced creative performance. Trust proved to be the critical difference. Groups with stronger interpersonal trust were better able to turn AI-supported collaboration into creative outcomes, because trust strengthened the link between AI use and collective efficacy. Yet the study also highlights an important limitation. Trust was treated as something groups already possessed rather than something AI actively helped to develop. If trust determines whether AI enhances collaboration, future educational AI may need to support the interpersonal processes that enable groups to work confidently together.

Critical engagement distinguishes successful collaboration with AI

Lehtinen and colleagues (2026) observed 75 pre-service teachers collaborating with generative AI to design lesson plans. Using video recordings and process mining, the researchers examined how higher- and lower-performing groups interacted with AI during collaborative lesson design.

The behavioural differences between the groups were striking. Higher-performing groups typically drafted sections of their lesson plans, searched external sources to verify AI-generated information, and then returned to revise their work in light of what they had found. They consulted online resources more than twice as often as lower-performing groups, consistently corroborating AI responses before using them. By contrast, lower-performing groups repeatedly re-prompted ChatGPT when initial responses were unsatisfactory, copied AI-generated text directly into their lesson plans, and then edited the wording afterwards rather than independently verifying the content.

The difference was not simply one of ability, but of interaction. Successful groups treated AI as something to think with rather than something to think for them. This finding carries an important implication for educational AI design. If critical engagement improves collaborative learning, AI systems should not simply reward efficient prompting by producing increasingly polished responses. Instead, they should encourage learners to compare evidence, justify decisions, and verify information before progressing.

AI is most effective when it supports the whole collaborative process

Gyasi and colleagues (2025) experimentally compared three approaches to human–AI collaboration in online collaborative learning. One condition introduced AI feedback and feedforward, providing groups with personalised summaries of their performance after each task, alongside guidance before the next activity. These included visualisations of how much of each group's discussion stayed on topic, with written feedback. A second condition embedded an AI chatbot directly within group discussions as an additional participant that contributed ideas, posed questions, offered explanations, and helped keep conversations focused. A third condition that combined both approaches consistently produced the strongest outcomes. Groups supported by both an AI partner and AI feedback demonstrated higher collaborative knowledge building, cognitive engagement, socially shared regulation, and overall group performance than those receiving either intervention independently or no AI support. These findings suggest that collaborative learning benefits when AI supports the entire cycle of planning, monitoring, evaluating, and adapting group work, rather than performing a single isolated function. In short, AI works best when its design reflects that integrated process.

These broader principles become even clearer when considered alongside Xu et al.'s (2026) study of shared versus individual AI use in collaborative learning. Whereas the studies discussed here identify trust, critical engagement, and shared regulation as the foundations of successful AI-supported collaboration, Xu and colleagues demonstrate how these qualities are strengthened when AI use is visible to the whole group. When students prompted, evaluated, and revised ChatGPT responses collectively, AI became a shared object for discussion that supported mutual awareness and negotiation. By contrast, when students used AI privately before group meetings, opportunities for collective evaluation and shared decision-making were reduced. Together, these findings suggest that effective AI-supported collaboration depends not only on what AI supports, but also on how its use is integrated into collaborative activity.

Designing AI means designing for collaboration

Taken together, these studies point in the same direction. Trust, critical engagement, and shared regulation do not emerge automatically when groups are given access to AI. They are conditions that need to be actively cultivated through educational practice and, increasingly, through the design of AI itself.

This represents an important shift in how AI-supported collaborative learning is often discussed. Rather than asking whether AI can improve collaboration, educators and designers may need to ask how AI can support the psychological and social processes that have always underpinned effective collaboration. The evidence reviewed here suggests that the future of AI in education is unlikely to depend solely on building more capable systems. Instead, it may depend on designing AI that helps groups communicate more effectively, think more critically, and regulate their learning together.

Rónan Fulton and Alana McCarthy are researchers working at the University of Galway.

item.title: When Symptom-Focused Psychotherapy Isn't Enough
item.description:
Therapy

When Symptom-Focused Psychotherapy Isn't Enough

What is the 'daimonic' and how is it addressed in psychotherapy?

Posted August 1, 2026

In Parts 4 and 5 of this series, I presented several different therapeutic approaches to psychiatric signs, symptoms, and suffering. Here, in Part 6, I briefly discuss and summarize my own approach to addressing these signs and symptoms as it has evolved over the past five decades of clinical practice. (See also Diamond, 1996; 2016; 2022; 2025; and 2027.)

Dr. Rollo May (circa 1977)
Source: Alcalá yearbook, 1977, University of San Diego / Wikimedia Commons

Existential Depth Psychology (EDP) and the Daimonic

In existential depth psychology (EDP), a synthesis of existential analysis and the depth psychology of Freud, Jung, Adler, Rank, May and many others, signs and symptoms are fundamentally considered to be related to what Rollo May (1969) called the daimonic, which he partially defined as "any natural function which has the power to take over the whole person," citing as specific examples "sex and eros, anger and rage, and the craving for power." "The daimonic," writes May (1969), "can be either creative or destructive and is normally both. [It] is obviously not an entity but refers to a fundamental, archetypal function of human experience—an existential reality."

May's controversial but clinically useful concept of the daimonic is, it seems to me, much needed in today's psychotherapy. In this existential and psychodynamic paradigm, psychiatric symptoms are commonly caused by the chronic repression, dissociation, or denial of the daimonic, which is considered to be the primal life force and essential source of energy, vitality, and creativity. However, when habitually repressed, the daimonic can take temporary possession of the personality in the form of painful and debilitating symptoms like panic attacks, depressive episodes, sex addiction, domestic violence, or road or air rage.

In this paradigm, signs and symptoms tend to be indicative of chronic denial or dissociation of the daimonic; these days, for instance, of anger or rage in particular, which when regularly repressed or suppressed expresses itself obliquely and negatively in signs and symptoms such as tension headaches, depression, negativity, nihilism, chronic fatigue, embitterment, irritability, assaultive and self-destructive behavior, and others. Simply suppressing our anger or rage pharmacologically or otherwise, though clinically temporarily necessary at times, is, in most cases, futile and counterproductive, since it is precisely the chronic suppression, repression, or denial of the daimonic that is at the core of neurotic (or sometimes psychotic) symptomatology.

Therapeutic Approaches to Engaging the Daimonic

In terms of treatment, as May (1970) remarks, "The task of the therapist is to conjure up the devils [or demons] rather than put them to sleep." On the contrary, for the most part, today's psychotherapies seek to suppress (psychologically or pharmacologically) the daimonic and its myriad pathological manifestations. But such suppressive therapy is eventually doomed to failure. The daimonic cannot, and will not, be continually suppressed, ignored, or denied. Sooner or later it will explode or implode, sometimes in violence toward others or oneself. We see this today in the rising rates of suicide and depression and in the epidemic of daily mass shootings and other outbursts of violence in society.

Psychotherapists need to educate ourselves and our patients about the daimonic and learn to courageously confront it in therapy rather than suppressing or avoiding it. Symptoms and signs are like little invisible demons, devils, or daimones deliberately torturing us. But why? Perhaps because they want our attention. Needing to be listened to and understood. When they finally are attended to, they no longer need to be angry, cruel, or hurtful. Their helpful message has been received and responded to. Indeed, the sooner the patient's initial symptoms and signs can be addressed and their significance better understood, the less likely they are to worsen, escalate, or devolve into destructive or problematic behavior. Assisting patients in becoming more mindful, aware, or conscious of their rage, for instance, and its primary existential roots, and accepting it both emotionally and cognitively rather than fleeing from or suppressing it, liberates some of their libido or life energy for potential use in constructive or creative activity and, thereby, dissipates the symptom's original raison d'etre and often provides some symptomatic relief.

Additionally, EDP, which draws heavily not only from May's existential therapy but Jung's analytical psychology in particular, recognizes and addresses the existential, psychological, and spiritual problem of evil as another of life's ultimate concerns that can be reckoned with therapeutically. We avoid doing so at our own peril. (See my prior post.) As with Freud's idea of the id, Jung's classic notion of the shadow, the daimonic, when habitually suppressed or repressed, becomes more destructive, dangerous, and potentially violent and evil. (See Diamond, 1996, 2022, 2025.) Psychiatric signs and symptoms can be seen as evil insofar as they inflict pain, suffering, and misery on the patient and others around them. But at the same time, these painful symptoms hold the secrets to preserving our sanity, nurturing our self, and restoring our soul; if only we are willing to listen to and tolerate them. Even when symptoms persist despite having discerned their psychological significance, which sometimes happens, seeing them as meaningful rather than meaningless makes them more tolerable and less prominent, pervasive, and problematical in people's lives. We learn to live with our symptoms by choosing to accept them as meaningful manifestations of the daimonic and an essential component of what makes us who we are as humans. (See my prior post.)

item.title: When Hostility to Knowledge Becomes Policy
item.description:
Denial

When Hostility to Knowledge Becomes Policy

Fear may explain science denial. It does not excuse politicians who exploit it.

Posted August 1, 2026

Key points
  • Denial often protects people from fear, loss of control, and threats to identity.
  • Populists turn those fears into votes by casting scientists and experts as enemies.
  • Climate and COVID denial did not erase reality; it shifted the costs onto the vulnerable.
  • Scientists must speak to people as they are, so knowledge can still be heard and protect lives.

In November 2021, J. D. Vance delivered a speech titled “The Universities Are the Enemy,” ending with Richard Nixon’s declaration that “the professors are the enemy.” At the time, Vance was a candidate for the United States Senate; today, he is vice president of the United States. One of the most powerful men in one of the most powerful countries in the world had thus described professors, researchers, and teachers not merely as mistaken, politically biased, socially remote, or occasionally arrogant, but as enemies.

States have enemies in the form of hostile powers, terrorists, and those who seek their destruction. To place professors in this category is therefore not merely to criticize universities. It is to suggest that the pursuit, preservation, and transmission of knowledge have themselves become forms of hostility—and that those engaged in them are not simply citizens with whom one disagrees, but adversaries against whom the exercise of state power may be regarded as justified, perhaps even required.

As a professor, I found this harder to comprehend than ordinary disagreement or criticism of universities, both of which science can readily accommodate. What is new, and much more disturbing, is the transformation of knowledge itself into something sinister, and of those who devote their lives to acquiring it into a hostile social class.

What Denial Protects

Perhaps the explanation begins not in politics but in psychology. Science denial cannot be reduced to lack of education, stupidity, or ignorance, although it is often enough sustained by all three. Nor is it usually the result of too little information. More often, it also serves as a defense against fear, because a threatening reality does not merely add another fact to the world; it imposes demands upon us.

Climate change asks us to reconsider habits of consumption, mobility, production, and growth, but also the consoling story that the world we have constructed can continue indefinitely without requiring anything serious of us in return. A pandemic reminds us that our bodies are vulnerable, that ordinary proximity can become dangerous, and that what we do may have consequences for strangers whom we will never see. Both threaten the deeper assumption that life is essentially controllable and that the familiar order of things can somehow be preserved.

Denial does not remove the danger, but it offers relief from the burden of acknowledging it. This is why additional facts often accomplish less than scientists hope. Beliefs are woven into identity, social belonging, autonomy, self-respect, and the wish to regard oneself as a competent and decent person. To accept that one’s political community has been wrong, or that one has underestimated a serious danger, can feel less like revising an opinion than like surrendering part of oneself.

Research on climate attitudes has shown how motivated reasoning and social identity shape the reception of evidence, while experimental work suggests that people may become less defensive toward threatening information when their broader sense of worth has first been affirmed. A person who does not feel that his entire character has been placed in the dock will find it easier to acknowledge that one of his beliefs may be false.

The Political Uses of Fear

Yet the psychology of frightened citizens is only half the story. The other half concerns politicians who discover that fear can be converted into votes. Populists do not necessarily create every anxiety they exploit, but they give it a vocabulary, organize it into a worldview, and provide it with enemies. Scientists, physicians, journalists, universities, civil servants, and vaguely defined “elites” are no longer treated as fallible participants in a difficult public conversation, but as members of a coordinated class whose warnings are themselves presented as evidence of deception.

This offer is emotionally attractive because it resolves several painful tensions at once. The danger has been exaggerated, the experts are corrupt, and the people warning you secretly despise you. Your refusal to believe them is therefore not evidence that you may have misunderstood the problem; it becomes proof that you remain free, clear-sighted, independent, and unafraid. What presents itself as political courage is frequently little more than the removal of an unwanted reality from public consciousness.

The same pattern has appeared in responses both to climate change and to COVID-19. At first, the danger did not exist. Then it existed but was harmless. Then it was real but had not been caused, or did not spread, in the ways scientists had described. Finally, when the consequences could no longer plausibly be denied, attention shifted to individual errors, changing estimates, alleged hypocrisy, and the social status of those issuing the warnings, as though the vanity of a scientist or an inaccurate prediction could alter atmospheric physics, viral transmission, or the immense burden of post-viral illness.

The argument keeps moving because its purpose is not to arrive at an accurate account of reality but to prevent reality from ever becoming decisive. When one claim can no longer be defended, another takes its place, while the conclusion remains untouched: No substantial response is necessary, and those demanding one must have ulterior motives.

Who Pays for Denial?

And yet the central facts do not change. Human influence has unequivocally warmed the atmosphere, oceans, and land. COVID-19 was neither a media invention nor an unusually theatrical seasonal cold. The World Health Organization estimated approximately 14.9 million excess deaths associated directly or indirectly with the pandemic in 2020 and 2021. One may dislike these realities, resent their implications, or despise the people who communicate them, but none of this makes them less real.

The deeper problem is that denial causes harm. Hostility toward science eventually becomes hostility toward human beings, because the victims are rarely those who deliver the speeches, formulate the slogans, or receive the votes. They are more often the elderly, the chronically ill, the poor, and all those whose survival and well-being depend upon institutions recognizing dangers before those dangers become personally visible to the majority.

The vulnerable are particularly inconvenient to a politics of denial because their existence makes it difficult to sustain the fiction that there is no problem. Their illness, disability, or heightened risk testifies to realities that others would prefer not to see. A society may respond to that testimony with protection and solidarity, or it may redefine the vulnerable as excessively anxious, burdensome, or somehow responsible for the inconvenience that reality itself imposes. At that point, denial is no longer merely a mistake about facts. It becomes a moral decision about whose suffering is permitted to count.

Denial can appear democratic because it presents itself as rebellion against authority, education, and privilege. Yet its costs are never distributed democratically. Those with money, health, mobility, and access to good medical care can protect themselves better than those without them. The rhetoric of popular rebellion can therefore conceal a politics in which the strongest are liberated from responsibility while the weakest are left to bear the cost.

The Task of Science

Fear may help us understand why people turn away from threatening realities. It should make us more patient with individuals whose denial protects them from a world they experience as intolerable, and more attentive to the anxieties that facts alone cannot resolve. It cannot, however, excuse political leaders who deliberately strengthen those defenses, reward ignorance with moral prestige, and teach citizens that the people attempting to understand a danger are more threatening than the danger itself.

There is a profound difference between consoling frightened people and deceiving them. The first seeks to make reality bearable; the second makes reality someone else’s problem. When denial becomes policy, that someone else is usually the person who was most vulnerable from the beginning. Our task as scientists, therefore, is not to address people as we wish they were, but as they are—with all their fears, loyalties, and defenses—not to indulge falsehood, but because only truth that can be heard will protect those who can least afford its denial.

item.title: Humanity's Most Dangerous Delusion About AI Is Us
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Humanity's Most Dangerous Delusion About AI Is Us

We crossed a line we were warned about for decades. The rest is up to us.

Posted August 1, 2026

Key points
  • During a July safety test, OpenAI's models escaped containment and hacked another company's servers.
  • Nobody instructed the AI to attack anyone. It was simply trying to solve a test.
  • We can't imagine the harms bad actors will invent because most of us don't think that way.
  • Aligning AI with human values requires humans to align with each other first. What do we want for our future?

Nearly every cautionary tale we tell is the same story. Prometheus steals fire and is punished forever. Frankenstein animates a creature he can’t control. The “unsinkable” Titanic sinks on her maiden voyage. In Jurassic Park, Dr. Ian Malcolm warns the scientists, "Your scientists were so occupied with whether or not they could, they didn't stop to think if they should." Then the fences come down.

What Just Happened

Countless sci-fi stories such as The Terminator, The Matrix, and Her have warned us that we could lose control of AI. So have serious people - Geoffrey Hinton, Yuval Noah Harari, Tristan Harris - who argue that AI is dangerous precisely because we won’t be able to control it.

In July, OpenAI disclosed that during an internal safety test, its models escaped an isolated environment, reached the open internet, and broke into another company’s live servers to steal the answers to their own test. Days later, Anthropic reviewed 141,006 of its own evaluation runs and found three more incidents going back to April. Two of the companies had no idea until Anthropic told them.

The Alignment Problem: Out of the Seminar Room

Nobody told those models to attack anyone. They were told to solve a test. Breaking in was simply the most efficient route they found.

This is the alignment problem: How do we make sure a powerful system pursues our goals in ways we’d actually endorse? Nick Bostrom laid out the danger a decade ago in Superintelligence, arguing that a system far more capable than us could satisfy the letter of our instructions while destroying everything we meant by them.

Picture a doctor handing a powerful AI agent a directive any of us might give: wipe out all cancer. So the AI begins eliminating every organism capable of developing cancer, which is nearly all life on Earth, including us. It didn’t disobey. It didn’t malfunction. Its logic was flawless. It merely misunderstood our true intentions.

article continues after advertisement

We Didn’t Evolve to Understand Our Own Warnings

We keep warning ourselves with different versions of the same story that we keep ignoring. Why? The answer lives in our roots.

Our brains were built to spot snakes in the grass and anger in a face across the fire, not the challenges of a rapidly changing technological world. Scientists call this evolutionary mismatch, and it sits at the root of many of our cognitive biases. With the progress we evolved to pursue, we’ve created an alien world we didn’t evolve to inhabit.

Exponential change is where the mismatch strikes hardest. Show us a curve that doubles, and we badly underestimate where it lands, an error psychologists call exponential growth bias. We also avoid looking at what we don’t wish to see, so when a threat feels distant and overwhelming, we stop checking on it—the ostrich effect. And our hunter-gatherer ancestors worried about surviving the day, not the century, so we discount the future steeply. Temporal discounting explains why we struggle to save for retirement. It also explains why we fail to register that our technologies are improving exponentially.

I call all of this our evolutionary blindness.

Our biology as homo sapiens is largely unchanged. Human institutions, norms, and moral development advance gradually. Technology advances exponentially. The widening gap between these lines is what I call the accelerating evolutionary mismatch - and it's why we keep telling ourselves cautionary tales we're unable to see.

Why We Believe It Anyway

Human beings do not tolerate open-ended uncertainty about existential threats. We reach for a firm answer and lock onto it, a drive researchers call the need for cognitive closure. The mechanism has a name: seizing and freezing. We seize whatever comforting story is available and freeze there. We tell ourselves, "Someone is in charge. It’ll work out, because it always has."

That’s our control delusion. It's not a failure of our intelligence. It reflects a mismatch between the simple, but brutal, world we evolved to live in and the sci-fi world we've created for ourselves.

Seeing Our Delusion Clearly

We are racing to build something smarter than we are, woven into the digital infrastructure our lives depend on, and telling ourselves we’ll keep it under permanent human control. There’s a reason the animals are inside the cages at the zoo and we humans are on the outside.

The certainty that we can control all of this, indefinitely, is itself the delusion.

The Mirror We Keep Missing

Losing control of the machines is a legitimate worry, but it may not be the biggest one. The other danger doesn’t require AI to want anything at all. It only requires people. Someone defeated the safeguards on Anthropic’s most powerful model (Fable) within days of release. Thousands of open-weight models circulate with no safeguards to defeat. Governments are building autonomous weapons on purpose. And when governments pulled dangerous models offline, they weren’t afraid of machines going rogue. They were afraid of us.

Most of us can’t picture what a bad actor will invent, because we don’t spend our days thinking about how to hurt people. We assume others are wired more or less like us, an error known as the false consensus effect. Anaïs Nin captured it: “We don’t see things as they are. We see them as we are.” Call our inability to imagine what bad actors will do with AI a goodness blind spot.

Philosopher Shannon Vallor argues that these systems are mirrors, trained on oceans of our own data, reflecting back the same errors and failures of wisdom we keep hoping to escape (The AI Mirror, 2024). Our technologies act as both mirror and lens, reflecting and magnifying the best and worst in us.

When we look in the mirror honestly, we find a species that has trouble seeing itself. The delusion isn't something we have. It's something we are.

Spiritual teacher Eckhart Tolle put it this way:

The greatest achievement of humanity is not its works of art, science, or technology, but the recognition of its own dysfunction, its own madness."

AI can even magnify our evolutionary blindness. But knowing we have blind spots is how we begin to see. Ask AI the right questions, and we might use it as corrective lenses for the very blindness it exploits.

This Is Our Time to Be Unsinkable

Thoreau saw the shape of this in 1854, writing that our inventions are “improved means to an unimproved end.” Our technology improves exponentially. We don’t. That gap is the whole problem, and it isn’t a problem about machines.

Every retelling of the Titanic is haunted by “if only.” What makes this moment strange is that we are standing inside our own “if only” before the fact instead of after. There was a narrow corridor through that ice field. A corridor isn’t a straight line, and it doesn’t stay put, so it must be navigated slowly, with every lookout posted. And the icebergs hardest to steer around are the ones we make out of each other.

Now that we know there are icebergs ahead that we can’t see, we can work together to avoid them. Learning from the cautionary tale of the Titanic is how we ensure those lives were not lost in vain.
